mainline-protestant-pcusa-elca-umc.in_a_sentence: Three of the largest American denominations, Presbyterian, Lutheran and Methodist, sharing printed liturgies, infant baptism and ordained women. All three read Scripture alongside the creeds, scholarship and the church’s long experience.
what_marks_it_out: The Table is the clearest mark. All three teach that God actually gives something in the sacraments rather than merely reminding you of something, and all three baptise infants, which is why this sketch sits so far towards the sacramental end.

On grace the map names nothing, and that is honest rather than evasive. Three inheritances share one band: Lutherans who say conversion is God’s work alone, Presbyterians who confess election, Methodists who say grace reaches everyone and can be refused. Nobody here is made to choose.

Authority picks no side either. Scripture comes first in all three governing books, but so does reading it with the creeds, with scholarship and with the church’s experience, which Methodists shorten to Scripture, tradition, reason and experience. Neither “the Bible alone” nor “the Bible plus a teaching office” fits.

Worship leans liturgical without being fixed: service books and a church year, followed closely in one congregation and lightly in the next. None of the three has ever taught that the gifts of the Spirit ceased, though tongues are not expected either, so that reading sits open.

One more thing ties the three together on a Sunday morning. All three commend the Revised Common Lectionary, the three-year cycle of set readings published in 1992 and built on the Roman Catholic lectionary of 1969, so a Presbyterian, a Lutheran, a Methodist and a Catholic can hear much the same Scripture on the same day. All three ordain women, which is one of the plainest lines between this family and the conservative evangelical bodies.

did_you_know.text: The PCUSA does not have a confession; it has twelve, bound into a Book of Confessions running from the Nicene Creed to the Confession of Belhar, the short statement written in South Africa against apartheid and added in 2016.
did_you_know.source: PC(USA) 222nd General Assembly, 2016, adopting Belhar as the twelfth confession; PC(USA) Book of Confessions.

did_you_know.text: Between 2019 and the end of 2023 more than 7,600 congregations, about a quarter of the total, left the United Methodist Church under a temporary exit rule that expired on 31 December 2023.
did_you_know.source: UMC Book of Discipline ¶2553, expired 31 December 2023; Christianity Today, December 2023.

mainline-protestant-pcusa-elca-umc.family: Each came out of the Reformation by a different door: the ELCA from Luther, the PCUSA from Calvin by way of Scotland, the UMC from Wesley and the Church of England. They are near relatives by agreement as well as descent: the ELCA has been in full communion with the PCUSA since 1997, the Episcopal Church since 2001 and the UMC since 2009, so their ministers can serve in each other’s churches.

read.placed_from: PCUSA Book of Confessions and Book of Order W-3; ELCA "The Use of the Means of Grace" (1997); UMC Book of Discipline.

open.title: The Use of the Means of Grace (ELCA, 1997)
open.note: Short and practical: the plainest account of why these churches sit where they do on baptism and communion.

open.title: The Confession of Belhar (1986)
open.note: Two pages written against apartheid, now one of the twelve confessions a PCUSA minister promises to be guided by.

national-baptist-nbc-usa-historically-bl.in_a_sentence: The largest historically Black Baptist body in the United States, made of self-governing congregations with no creed but the Bible. Worship is built on preaching and song, and baptism is the immersion of people who already believe.
what_marks_it_out: Two readings sit almost at the edge. Authority is Scripture alone: no creed binds a National Baptist congregation, and the Articles of Faith are a summary a church may adopt, not a court. The Supper is a memorial, and baptism the immersion of someone who already believes.

On grace the sketch leans towards free response, and the paperwork says why. The Articles follow the New Hampshire Confession of 1833, whose sixth article makes salvation free to all and blames nothing but a sinner’s own refusal, while its eleventh insists real believers are kept to the end by God’s power.

Worship is as free as this map goes: no prayer book, no set order, the shape coming from the preacher, a congregation answering out loud, and the music. In many older churches the devotional before the sermon still carries “Dr Watts” singing, where a leader intones one line and the room returns it.

Nothing in the Articles says the Spirit’s gifts have stopped, and the expectation that He is at work on a Sunday is real, but speaking in tongues is not the marker it is in a Pentecostal church. The dispensational lean, a literal future for Israel, comes from generations of American Baptist preaching rather than from any confession.

Behind that grace reading stands a document most American Baptists have inherited without noticing. The New Hampshire Confession of 1833 was written to be gentler about election than the older Calvinist Baptist confessions, and it travelled: into the South, into the Black conventions, and into the statement the Southern Baptists adopted in 1925. It is why a National Baptist and a Southern Baptist who have never met often describe being saved in nearly the same words.

did_you_know.text: The convention was born in a single day. On 24 September 1895, at Friendship Baptist Church in Atlanta, three Black Baptist organisations (foreign missions, home missions and education) merged into one body and became its three boards.
did_you_know.source: American Baptist Historical Society, “National Baptist Convention, USA, Inc Organized in Atlanta”; BlackPast, “National Baptist Convention (1895– )”.

did_you_know.text: In 1961 a fight over how long a president could serve, and over Martin Luther King Jr’s direct-action campaigns, broke the convention apart. That November 33 ministers formed the Progressive National Baptist Convention, which King, Ralph Abernathy and Gardner Taylor joined.
did_you_know.source: Martin Luther King, Jr. Research and Education Institute, Stanford; BlackPast, “Progressive National Baptist Convention (1961– )”.

national-baptist-nbc-usa-historically-bl.family: Baptist by descent, through the English Separatists and the American revivals, but organised separately: Black Baptists built and ran their own conventions rather than stay junior partners in anyone else’s. Its nearest relatives are the other National Baptist bodies, one of which split away in 1915 in a quarrel over who owned the publishing house, and, in doctrine if not in the sound of a service, the Southern Baptists.

read.placed_from: National Baptist Convention USA Articles of Faith; New Hampshire Confession (1833), the Baptist confession behind them.

open.title: The New Hampshire Confession of Faith (1833)
open.note: A page and a half. Article 6 on the freeness of salvation and article 11 on perseverance carry the grace reading.

open.title: National Baptist Convention USA Articles of Faith
open.note: The convention’s own summary, short enough to read in a sitting, and the source of all six readings here.

pentecostal-assemblies-of-god-church-of-.in_a_sentence: Churches born out of the revivals of the early 1900s, which expect the Holy Spirit to act audibly and visibly now. Tongues, prophecy and healing are looked for today, as they happen in Acts.
what_marks_it_out: The gifts reading sits as far over as the map goes, which is the whole point. The Assemblies of God teaches that baptism in the Holy Spirit is a distinct experience after conversion, “witnessed by the initial physical sign of speaking with other tongues”. It is the normal Christian inheritance, not a prize for the unusually holy.

On grace Pentecostals stand firmly on the free-response side. Grace comes first and reaches everyone, each person has to say yes, and most Pentecostal bodies hold that someone can later walk away, so assurance is real but is not a sealed verdict.

Worship is free to the edge of the scale: no prayer book, no set readings, a service that can change shape in the room. The Table matches it. The Supper is a memorial of the Lord’s suffering and death, and baptism is for people old enough to ask for it.

On Israel and the church this is openly dispensational, and the statements say so rather than leaving it to custom: the Fundamental Truths name “the Blessed Hope”, the church caught up before the tribulation, and a millennial reign that includes the salvation of national Israel. Authority is Scripture alone, argued from Acts rather than from a council.

Assemblies of God congregations sum the whole thing up in four cardinal doctrines: salvation, baptism in the Holy Spirit, divine healing, and the second coming. Healing is the one most visible from a pew. Prayer for the sick is not tucked into a quiet slot midweek. It happens at the front, out loud, with hands laid on, because these churches hold that healing is provided for in Christ’s atonement and is meant for now.

did_you_know.text: The founding moment had no denomination behind it: a revival that began in 1906 in a run-down mission at 312 Azusa Street, Los Angeles, led by William J. Seymour, the son of former slaves, with Black and white worshippers together in a segregated city.
did_you_know.source: Flower Pentecostal Heritage Center, AG History; Assemblies of God (USA), “History”.

did_you_know.text: The three bodies here began in three different decades: the Church of God at Barney Creek, Tennessee, on 19 August 1886; the Church of God in Christ, organised by Charles Harrison Mason in 1907 after he received the Spirit at Azusa Street; the Assemblies of God at Hot Springs, Arkansas, in April 1914.
did_you_know.source: Church of God (Cleveland, Tennessee) published history; COGIC history; Assemblies of God (USA), “History” (Hot Springs, 2–12 April 1914).

pentecostal-assemblies-of-god-church-of-.family: Pentecostalism grew from the Wesleyan holiness movement, which is why its account of grace still sounds like Wesley, and from the Azusa Street revival, which gave it tongues. Downstream are the charismatic and non-denominational churches, which took the gifts without the denominations. The “Oneness” Pentecostals, who baptise in Jesus’ name only and reject the doctrine of the Trinity, separated in the 1910s and are not what this sketch describes.

read.placed_from: Assemblies of God Statement of Fundamental Truths 1, 6, 7, 8, 13, 14; Church of God (Cleveland) Declaration of Faith.

open.title: Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths
open.note: Sixteen short articles. Numbers 7 and 8 cover Spirit baptism and tongues; 13 and 14 cover the rapture and the millennium.

open.title: Church of God (Cleveland, Tennessee), Declaration of Faith
open.note: Fourteen single sentences on one page, and a quick way to tell shared Pentecostal ground from one body’s own.

presbyterian-reformed-confessional.in_a_sentence: Churches governed by elders and bound to the Westminster Confession or the Three Forms of Unity. God’s choosing comes first, one covenant runs from Abraham to the font, and worship does only what Scripture commands.
what_marks_it_out: Grace sits at the far monergist edge, monergism being the view that God alone brings a person to believe. Westminster says God chose a people before the world was made, and that the grace which raises the spiritually dead makes the unwilling willing. Because the work is His, so is finishing it.

Covenant theology holds the rest together. One people of God runs across both testaments under one covenant of grace, so there is no separate track for Israel and no rapture in the system, and the children of believers are baptised as Abraham’s children were marked. At the Table Christ is really given, but spiritually rather than physically.

The cessationist reading comes from the Confession’s first paragraph, which says the older ways God used to reveal His will are “now ceased”. The claim is not that He has stopped healing, but that He has stopped adding to Scripture.

The worship reading surprises people. Presbyterians look formal, yet the map puts them on the free side of centre, correctly: the Westminster Assembly replaced the Book of Common Prayer with a Directory, which is advice rather than words to read aloud, and nothing enters a service unless Scripture calls for it.

The name is the government. Presbyteros is the Greek for elder, and these churches are run by elders: a session of them in each congregation, a presbytery of ministers and elders over a region, and a general assembly above that. There is no bishop, and no congregation stands entirely on its own, so a minister answers to a court of his peers rather than to the people who pay him.

did_you_know.text: The Confession took three years, and the committee that wrote it never really stopped. Parliament summoned 121 ministers to Westminster Abbey in July 1643; they moved into the Jerusalem Chamber that October, finished the Confession in 1646, and had held 1,163 numbered sessions by the time they stopped counting in 1649. The minutes run on to 1652.

The Heidelberg Catechism of 1563 is a calendar as well as a book: its 129 questions are cut into fifty-two Lord’s Days so a congregation hears all of it preached once a year. It opens by asking “What is your only comfort in life and in death?”
did_you_know.source: Heidelberg Catechism (1563), Lord’s Day 1; Christian Reformed Church, “Heidelberg Catechism”.

presbyterian-reformed-confessional.family: Geneva is the taproot, through Calvin and then John Knox’s Scotland. The English-speaking branch confesses Westminster, finished in 1646; the Dutch and German branch confesses the Belgic Confession, the Heidelberg Catechism and the Canons of Dort. Nearest relatives: Reformed Baptists, who copied Westminster and then rewrote its chapters on baptism, and confessional Lutherans, who share the monergism and part company at the Table.

read.placed_from: Westminster Confession 1.1, 3, 10, 21.5, 28-29, 31.3-4; Westminster Directory for Publick Worship; Heidelberg Catechism 65-82.

open.title: The Westminster Confession of Faith (1646)
open.note: Thirty-three short chapters. Chapter 1 carries authority and cessation, chapter 3 grace, and 21.5 worship.

open.title: The Heidelberg Catechism (1563)
open.note: Warmer than the Confession and far shorter. Questions 65 to 82, on the sacraments, hold up the Table reading.

reformed-baptist-1689.in_a_sentence: Calvinists who baptise believers rather than babies, holding Westminster’s doctrine of grace, covenant and Scripture. Baptists rewrote that confession in 1677, changing its chapters on baptism and church government and little else.
what_marks_it_out: Four of the six readings here are simply Westminster’s, because the 1689 Confession borrowed Westminster’s words for them: grace monergist to the edge, the gifts ceased, authority Scripture alone, and Israel and the church one people under one covenant of grace.

The Table reading is what makes this tradition itself, and it lands in the middle where the map names nothing. The Confession says believers at the Supper “really and indeed, yet not carnally and corporally, but spiritually, receive and feed upon Christ crucified”, which is Calvin’s language and well above bare remembrance. Yet the same churches baptise only professing believers, and usually preach the Supper as a memorial.

The baptism difference is not a detail bolted onto a Presbyterian frame. Presbyterians baptise infants because believers’ children belong to the covenant as Abraham’s did; the 1689 rewrote that chapter to say the covenant does not pass down by descent. It is entered by faith, and the sign belongs to those who have it.

Worship is free and deliberately so. Nothing enters a service that Scripture does not call for, and each congregation governs itself, so there is no prayer book, no bishop and no imposed order. The result is plain, long on preaching, heavy on singing everyone can join.

The older name for this stream is Particular Baptist, and the word carries the doctrine: particular redemption, the teaching that Christ died to save a particular people rather than to make everyone savable. The General Baptists, who held that He died for everyone, were the other English Baptist family, and the two ran side by side for two centuries. Government is congregational, with elders and deacons and nobody above the local church.

did_you_know.text: The confession was published anonymously in 1677, while Nonconformist meetings were illegal, with no authors’ names and no printer’s name on it. Only after the Toleration Act could thirty-seven ministers sign it, in London in September 1689, which is why it carries the later date.
did_you_know.source: The 1677 and 1689 editions; Reformation Today, “Baptist Confession Making 1644 and 1689”.

did_you_know.text: Charles Spurgeon reprinted it in October 1855, in his second year in London, telling his congregation it was “not issued as an authoritative rule, or code of faith, whereby you are to be fettered” but as help in an argument.
did_you_know.source: Spurgeon’s 1855 preface, “To All the Household of Faith”.

reformed-baptist-1689.family: English Particular Baptists, out of the same Puritan congregationalism as the Independents, keeping its Calvinism and dropping infant baptism. Its immediate parent is not Westminster but the Savoy Declaration of 1658, the Congregationalists’ revision of Westminster, which supplied most of the 1689’s actual wording. Living relatives: confessional Presbyterians, and today’s Calvinist Southern Baptists.

open.title: The Second London Baptist Confession (1677/1689)
open.note: Chapter 7 on the covenant and chapters 28 to 30 on baptism and the Supper are the whole difference from Westminster.

open.title: The Savoy Declaration (1658)
open.note: The Congregationalist revision most of the 1689’s wording came from. Read side by side to see what Baptists changed.

reformed-charismatic-sovereign-grace-new.in_a_sentence: Churches that hold Calvin’s doctrine of grace and expect prophecy, tongues and healing in the same meeting. For most of the twentieth century that combination was assumed to be impossible.
what_marks_it_out: Two readings sit at opposite edges and both are at a pole. Grace is monergist, meaning God alone brings a person to believe, and election is taught here as warmly as in any Presbyterian church. The gifts are continuationist: prophecy in a Sunday meeting, prayer for healing out loud, speaking in tongues treated as normal.

It holds together because of the authority reading, which sits at the Scripture-alone end. A prophecy here is not new revelation and carries no weight against the Bible: it is tested, it can be wrong, and the canon is closed. That is what lets a Reformed church welcome prophecy without becoming Pentecostal.

The Table reading lands in the middle, where the map names nothing: these churches baptise believers rather than infants, which pulls one way, and speak of the Supper as more than a memory exercise, which pulls the other. On Israel and the church the language is Reformed, with no rapture timetable.

Worship is free, loud and largely sung: no prayer book, no set readings, long stretches of congregational singing, preaching, and time left open for whatever the Spirit prompts. Sovereign Grace Music has been writing songs for that shape of service since the 1980s.

Government is by elders rather than by a congregational vote or a presbytery, and above the elders sit travelling leaders who plant churches and appoint them. Newfrontiers is willing to call that ministry apostolic, on the grounds that Ephesians 4:11 names apostles alongside prophets, evangelists and shepherds. It is not a claim to stand with the Twelve and it adds nothing to Scripture. It is a claim that the work of starting churches never ended.

did_you_know.text: The two halves share a grandparent. Both grew out of the British house church movement: Terry Virgo began with a small congregation in Seaford, on the English south coast, in 1968, and the Americans who founded Sovereign Grace in 1982 were shaped by the same British leaders.
did_you_know.source: Terry Virgo and Newfrontiers’ published history; Sovereign Grace Churches’ own history (People of Destiny International, 1982).

did_you_know.text: The label sounds like a contradiction because for decades it was treated as one: Reformed teachers were almost all cessationist and charismatics almost all Arminian. Wayne Grudem’s Systematic Theology (1994) became the standard case that a closed canon and continuing prophecy can live together.
did_you_know.source: Terry Virgo, interview on the distinctives of Newfrontiers; Grudem, Systematic Theology, chs. 52–53.

reformed-charismatic-sovereign-grace-new.family: Two roots twisted together: the charismatic renewal and the British new church movement of the 1960s and 70s gave it the gifts; the Reformed recovery of the same years (the Puritan reprints, the Banner of Truth, Lloyd-Jones’s London pulpit) gave it the doctrine of grace. Near relatives: non-denominational charismatics, who have the gifts without the Calvinism, and Reformed Baptists, who have the Calvinism without the gifts.

read.placed_from: Sovereign Grace Churches Statement of Faith; Newfrontiers "What We Believe"; Grudem, Systematic Theology chs. 52-53.

open.title: Sovereign Grace Churches, Statement of Faith
open.note: The clearest place to see both halves side by side: election in one article, the gifts of the Spirit a few lines later.

open.title: Newfrontiers, “What We Believe”
open.note: The British half of the family on one page, and the document behind the worship and authority readings here.

southern-baptist-calvinist.in_a_sentence: Southern Baptists who hold the doctrines of grace: election, effectual calling and perseverance. Everything around that is ordinary Baptist practice, with believer’s baptism, a memorial Supper and no bishop anywhere.
what_marks_it_out: Grace sits at the monergist edge, monergism being the view that God alone brings a person to believe, and it has a document behind it older than the argument. The Abstract of Principles of 1858 defines election as “God’s eternal choice of some persons unto everlasting life”, and every professor at Southern Seminary has taught in accordance with it since.

Everything else is plain Baptist, and three readings sit at the very edge. Authority is Scripture alone: no creed, no bishop and no convention binds a congregation. The Supper is “a symbolic act of obedience” remembering the Redeemer’s death, baptism is the immersion of a believer, and the order of service belongs to the church itself.

On Israel and the church the map names no position, and that is the convention’s doing. The Baptist Faith and Message says Jesus will return personally and visibly and that the dead will be raised and judged, then stops. It says nothing about a millennium or a rapture, so Calvinist Southern Baptists scatter right across that range.

The gifts reading leans cessationist without reaching the pole, which is honest: no Southern Baptist confession says the gifts have ended. The practice is simply cautious, and the case in this stream is argued from the sufficiency of Scripture rather than from a rule.

The recovery has been as much about how a church is run as about election. Founders Ministries, and later Mark Dever’s 9Marks, pressed for membership that means something, church discipline that is actually used, and preaching that works through a book of the Bible rather than around a theme. That is usually the first thing a visitor notices, long before anybody mentions Calvin.

did_you_know.text: Southern Baptists run two confessions at once: the Abstract of Principles of 1858, which binds one seminary’s faculty and is mildly Calvinist, and the Baptist Faith and Message of 2000, the convention’s own statement, written broadly enough to hold both sides.
did_you_know.source: SBTS “Fundamental Laws”, charter of 30 April 1858; Baptist Faith and Message 2000.

did_you_know.text: The argument is smaller than the noise. When Lifeway Research polled Southern Baptist pastors in 2012, 30 per cent called their congregation Calvinist and exactly 30 per cent called it Arminian; 16 per cent personally held all five points.
did_you_know.source: Lifeway Research, “SBC Pastors Polled on Calvinism and Its Effect”, June 2012.

southern-baptist-calvinist.family: Southern Baptist, and older in the convention than the label suggests: several of the men who founded it in 1845 and wrote the Abstract in 1858 were Calvinists, the emphasis faded across the twentieth century, and Founders Ministries began pressing for its recovery after a prayer meeting in November 1982. Nearest relatives: the non-Calvinist Southern Baptists it shares a convention with, and Reformed Baptists, who hold the same doctrine inside a full confession.

read.placed_from: Abstract of Principles IV-VI; Baptist Faith & Message 2000 I, II, VII, VIII, X.

open.title: The Abstract of Principles (1858)
open.note: Twenty articles, about two pages. Articles 4 to 6, on providence, election and the fall, carry the grace reading.

open.title: The Baptist Faith and Message (2000)
open.note: The convention’s own statement. Article 10, on last things, is worth reading for what it leaves unsaid.

southern-baptist-non-calvinist.in_a_sentence: The traditional Southern Baptist answer on grace, named by a statement its own senior figures published in 2012. God’s call goes out to everyone, each person must decide, and everyone who truly decides is kept for good.
what_marks_it_out: The grace reading leans towards free response without reaching the pole, because of a very Baptist pairing. Grace goes to all and can be refused, which is synergism: the view that a person freely cooperates with the grace God gives, or in the plainer word, free will. But once someone truly believes, God keeps them, which is eternal security, or “once saved, always saved” in the phrase people actually use. Classical Arminians hold that a believer can fall away; these churches do not, so they reject both labels.

Three readings sit at the very edge, and they are the marks of a free church rather than of that argument. Authority is Scripture alone, with no creed and no bishop over a congregation. The Supper is a memorial and baptism the immersion of a believer. Worship belongs to the church, not to a book.

On Israel and the church the sketch leans dispensational: a distinct future for national Israel, and a church caught up in the rapture before a time of tribulation. The Baptist Faith and Message does not require it, since its article on last things settles nothing, but the expectation runs through the preaching and the study Bibles this stream grew up reading.

The gifts reading leans cessationist without reaching the pole. No confession says the gifts have ended; there is simply a long settled practice of not seeking them, and a conviction that Scripture is enough without them.

What all this looks like on a Sunday is the invitation. The service ends with the congregation standing, a hymn, and a call to come to the front and settle it now, which makes sense only if the decision is genuinely the hearer’s to make. Churches in the Calvinist stream have often dropped that moment, and when the two sides argue about it they are really arguing about the doctrine underneath.

did_you_know.text: This side of the argument has a founding date. On 30 May 2012 A Statement of the Traditional Southern Baptist Understanding of God’s Plan of Salvation went online, and within weeks it carried the names of five former presidents of the convention and two seminary presidents.
did_you_know.source: Statement published by Eric Hankins, 30 May 2012; Baptist Press, “Statement on Calvinism draws approval, criticism”, June 2012.

did_you_know.text: The convention tried to settle it with a committee. Frank Page, a non-Calvinist himself, assembled an advisory team whose seven-page report, Truth, Trust and Testimony in a Time of Tension, went to the 2013 convention in Houston and concluded that both sides belong.
did_you_know.source: SBC Calvinism Advisory Committee report, presented at the Southern Baptist Convention, Houston, June 2013.

southern-baptist-non-calvinist.family: Baptist by way of the American frontier revivals, where the gospel was offered to whoever happened to be in the tent, and Southern Baptist since the convention formed in 1845. Its nearest relative is the Calvinist stream it shares a convention, a hymnbook and a mission board with; beyond that, the independent Bible churches and other free-church evangelicals.

read.placed_from: Baptist Faith & Message 2000; "A Statement of the Traditional Southern Baptist Understanding of God's Plan of Salvation" (2012).

open.title: The Baptist Faith and Message (2000)
open.note: Article 4 on salvation and article 5 on God’s purpose of grace are the two this page’s grace reading turns on.

open.title: A Statement of the Traditional Southern Baptist Understanding of God’s Plan of Salvation (2012)
open.note: Ten short articles, each an affirmation followed by a denial: this side setting out its own terms.

wesleyan-methodist.in_a_sentence: The churches that came from John Wesley, where grace is offered to every person and can be refused by every person. They keep a high view of communion, and a confidence that God really can make someone holy in this life.
what_marks_it_out: Grace sits at the synergist pole, synergism being the view that a person freely cooperates with the grace God gives. Wesley’s word for the first move is prevenient grace, which runs ahead of any decision and reaches everyone, so nobody can say they were never offered the chance. Then the person answers, and may say no, which is what Wesleyans mean when they insist on free will.

The Table reading will surprise anyone who has only met Methodism at its most informal. Wesley preached a sermon arguing that a Christian should receive communion as often as he possibly can, and over his life he communicated on average about once every four or five days. Methodists baptise infants and teach the Supper as a means of grace.

Authority reads as Scripture over tradition rather than Scripture alone: Scripture is the rule, and the creeds, the Articles of Religion and the church’s experience are consulted without being made equal to it. Methodists shorten this to Scripture, tradition, reason and experience, a phrase whose inventor later said he regretted coining, because people read it as four equal legs.

This is one of the few older Protestant traditions that never turned cessationist: Wesley argued the miraculous gifts faded not because the church had outgrown them but because Christians’ love had grown cold. Worship leans liturgical, with service books and a church year from the Church of England alongside extempore prayer and loud hymn singing.

The confidence about holiness has a name: entire sanctification, or Christian perfection. Wesley did not mean that a Christian stops making mistakes. He meant that love for God and neighbour can come to fill a person so completely that nothing is left competing for the heart, and that it is worth expecting in this life rather than at death. He gathered the case in A Plain Account of Christian Perfection, which traces his thinking back to 1725.

did_you_know.text: Wesley decided to go public against predestination by casting lots. In 1739 he drew twice over whether to preach his sermon Free Grace, and the lot came up “preach and print”. Whitefield begged him not to, asking “what will be the consequences but controversy?”, and the revival split in two.
did_you_know.source: Wesley’s Journal, April 1739; Whitefield to Wesley, 25 June and 2 July 1739.

did_you_know.text: American Methodism’s doctrinal standard is an edited Church of England. In 1784 Wesley cut the Thirty-Nine Articles down to twenty-four for the Americans, dropping predestination and anything peculiarly English; the Americans then added a twenty-fifth recognising the government of the new United States.
did_you_know.source: Wesley’s Sunday Service (1784); the Twenty-Five Articles adopted at the Christmas Conference, Baltimore, 1784.

wesleyan-methodist.family: The Church of England is the parent: Wesley was an Anglican priest who never left, and who handed his American societies a prayer book and his own edit of the Articles. The children are many: the United Methodist Church and the bodies leaving it, the African Methodist Episcopal churches, the Church of the Nazarene, the Salvation Army. Pentecostalism is a grandchild.

read.placed_from: Wesley, "Free Grace" and "The Duty of Constant Communion"; Articles of Religion V, VIII, XVI-XVIII; UMC Book of Discipline (Scripture, tradition, reason, experience).

open.title: John Wesley, “The Duty of Constant Communion”
open.note: A few pages, drafted in his Oxford days, and the reason this tradition sits so far towards the sacramental end.

open.title: John Wesley, “Free Grace”
open.note: The 1739 sermon against predestination that split the revival, and the clearest statement of why grace reads as it does here.
